title: India Warns US That New Tariffs Over Russian Oil Could Damage Ties
excerpt: Hours after the US House passed a bill authorizing tariffs of up to 100% on top Russian oil buyers, New Delhi cautioned Washington that the move could strain the bilateral relationship and vowed to protect its energy security.
body:
• India warned Washington on Thursday that new US tariffs on buyers of Russian oil could impact bilateral ties, hours after the House of Representatives passed a sweeping sanctions and tariff bill.
  • The bill, now headed to President Donald Trump for his signature, authorizes tariffs of up to 100% on China, India and other countries to push them to cut dependence on Russian oil and gas, and extends sanctions on Iran.
  • The foreign ministry said New Delhi had "very clearly articulated" the implications to US interlocutors over recent months, and vowed to take "all necessary measures" to protect its trade and economic interests.
  • India, the world's third-biggest oil importer, is among the largest buyers of Russian crude, with imports hitting an 11-month high in April 2026.

New Delhi's Warning

India said on Thursday that it remained firmly committed to ensuring energy security for its people and would continue to source supplies from diverse sellers based on market dynamics — issuing the statement hours after the US House of Representatives passed legislation targeting buyers of Russian energy.

The Indian foreign ministry said it had noted the passage of the bill and warned that any such new moves could impact ties between the two countries. It added that New Delhi had raised the issue with various US interlocutors in recent months and had "very clearly articulated" the potential implications for the bilateral relationship and the international energy market.

"The Indian side has also made clear its determination to take all necessary measures to protect its trade and economic interests."

— Ministry of External Affairs, India, in a statement

The government said it would work closely with trade and industry bodies to deal with the implications of the legislation.

What the Bill Does

The House-passed bill is intended to increase economic pressure on Russia over its invasion of Ukraine. It authorizes President Donald Trump to impose stiff tariffs of up to 100% on countries — including India and China — to reduce their dependence on Russian oil and gas, and also extends sanctions on Iran. The bill now goes to Trump, who must sign it for it to become law.

The legislation does not automatically trigger the full 100% duty; it creates the legal framework for the administration to act. But it hands Trump a powerful tariff weapon aimed squarely at Beijing and New Delhi, the two largest buyers of Russian crude.

A Long-Running Standoff

India has repeatedly resisted Western pressure to scale back its oil trade with Russia, arguing that its large population and economy need secure, affordable and reliable energy supplies. New Delhi has called for an end to the war in Ukraine but has not condemned Moscow, and has kept buying discounted Russian crude since Western sanctions began in 2022.

The pressure is not new. India already faces steep US duties: trade analysts note Indian exports face a 50% US tariff, with 25 percentage points linked to purchases of Russian crude, according to the Global Trade Research Initiative. India's imports of Russian crude reached an 11-month high in April 2026,.

China, the other major target, has pushed back against the congressional move, while Russia's foreign ministry has accused Washington of pursuing a "neocolonial agenda" and interfering in the internal affairs of sovereign nations over its tariff measures.

Impact and Analysis

Economists warn the bill injects fresh uncertainty into India's growth outlook. Aditi Nayar, chief economist at ICRA, noted that the mere prospect of higher duties and the resulting market uncertainty poses a downside risk to India's economic outlook — even before any tariffs are actually imposed.

For Indian exporters, the stakes are concrete. If enacted and enforced, the new measures could become the highest US duty India has faced, compounding existing tariffs and complicating New Delhi's bid for a trade deal with Washington.

"The mere prospect of increased duties and the resulting market uncertainty poses a downside risk to India's economic outlook."

— Aditi Nayar, Chief Economist, ICRA

Diaspora Angle

For the diaspora, the standoff lands close to home: Indian-American business owners who import from India, professionals in energy and trade, and the broader US-India commercial corridor all have a direct stake in whether the tariff weapon stays holstered or gets used. A rupture in the trade relationship would ripple through supply chains that diaspora entrepreneurs depend on.

What's Next

The immediate question is whether Trump signs the bill — and if he does, whether he deploys the tariff authority or keeps it as leverage. New Delhi has signaled it will neither commit to cutting Russian purchases nor back down on energy security. With trade talks stalled, the coming weeks will show whether this becomes another managed pressure point — or the one that breaks the table.
